nodes.name: Functional requirement
nodes.description: A statement of what a system must do, such as letting a user upload a photo or cancel an order.
nodes.markdown:
A functional requirement is a statement of what a system must do: a user can upload a photo, a customer can cancel an order, an admin can export last month's invoices. It describes behaviour you can check with a yes or a no.

Functional requirements come first in a design because they determine the data and the operations. "Users post short messages and see posts from people they follow" already implies a store of users, a follow relationship, a store of posts and a timeline read. How that timeline gets built, for example with [fan-out on write](node:Fan-out%20on%20write), depends on what the feature has to show.

They are paired with [non-functional requirements](node:Non-functional%20requirement), which say how well the system must do those things. "Users can search products" is functional. "Search returns within 200 ms" is non-functional.

A short set of questions usually produces the list:

| Question                   | Example answer                             |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Who uses it?               | Shoppers, warehouse staff, support agents  |
| What can they do?          | Place an order, track it, request a refund |
| What data goes in and out? | Order lines in, order status out           |
| What is out of scope?      | Gift cards, third-party sellers            |

The out-of-scope row prevents a common failure. A team builds for weeks, then learns in review that "notifications" meant SMS as well as email, or that refunds had to support part of an order. Writing the list down and getting it confirmed exposes that disagreement while it is still inexpensive to fix.

Keep the list short during a design discussion. Pick the few operations that drive the architecture, and leave settings pages and profile edits aside unless they change the shape of the system.
quotes: Should the feed include reposts, or only original posts?
Nobody wrote that down. Let's settle the functional requirements before we argue about storage, because reposts change what each timeline has to hold.

nodes.name: Non-functional requirement
nodes.description: A measurable statement of how well a system must work, covering qualities like speed, availability, durability and cost.
nodes.markdown:
Where a [functional requirement](node:Functional%20requirement) says what a system must do, a non-functional requirement says how well it must do it. For "users can search products", the non-functional version is "95% of searches return within 200 ms at 5,000 searches per second".

These requirements shape the architecture more than the feature list does. A photo-sharing app for 50 people and one for 50 million have similar features and very different designs. A system that works in a demo and times out on launch day usually met its functional requirements and had no stated target for load.

| Quality                       | Example target                      | Design consequence                                                           |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Latency](node:Latency)       | 99% of page loads under 500 ms      | [Caches](node:Cache), fewer network hops                                     |
| [Throughput](node:Throughput) | 5,000 orders per second at peak     | [Horizontal scaling](node:Horizontal%20scaling), queues                      |
| Availability                  | 99.9% of requests succeed monthly   | Redundancy, no [single point of failure](node:Single%20point%20of%20failure) |
| Durability                    | A confirmed payment is never lost   | Replicated storage, backups                                                  |
| Consistency                   | Balance is correct after a transfer | Limits on caching and asynchronous updates                                   |
| Cost                          | Under a set monthly budget          | Smaller fleet, simpler components                                            |

Targets need numbers to be useful. "The system must be fast" cannot be tested and cannot settle an argument. A number also shows what a goal costs. An availability target of 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month, while 99.99% allows about 4 minutes, which is too short for a person to respond to most failures and generally requires automated failover.

The qualities also compete. Stronger consistency tends to raise latency, and higher availability raises cost. Ask which requirement wins when two conflict, because that answer decides many later design choices. A payment system and a social feed will answer differently.
quotes: Do we really need multi-region for the internal reporting tool?
Check the non-functional requirements. It needs 99.5% during office hours, so one region with a tested restore is enough.

nodes.name: Back-of-the-envelope estimation
nodes.description: A quick calculation with rounded numbers that sizes traffic, storage and bandwidth before any design decision is made.
nodes.markdown:
Back-of-the-envelope estimation is a quick calculation with rounded numbers that tells you the rough size of a system before you design it. The aim is the right order of magnitude. Knowing whether a service handles 10, 1,000 or 100,000 requests per second decides whether one server is enough or a distributed design is needed.

A useful shortcut is that a day has 86,400 seconds, which rounds to 100,000. Here is a worked estimate for a social app with 10 million daily users:

| Step | Quantity                         | Calculation                       | Result             |
| ---- | -------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------ |
| 1    | Reads per day                    | 10M users × 20 reads              | 200M               |
| 2    | Average reads                    | 200M ÷ 86,400 s                   | About 2,300/s      |
| 3    | Peak reads                       | 2,300/s × 3 (assumed peak factor) | About 7,000/s      |
| 4    | Writes per day                   | 10M users × 0.1 posts             | 1M, about 12/s     |
| 5    | Storage per year                 | 1M posts × 2 KB × 365             | About 730 GB       |
| 6    | Peak [bandwidth](node:Bandwidth) | 7,000/s × 50 KB                   | 350 MB/s, 2.8 Gbps |

The result already suggests a design. Reads outnumber writes 200 to 1, so this is a [read-heavy workload](node:Read-heavy%20workload) and a [cache](node:Cache) will help. Storage fits on one machine for years, so splitting the database across machines is not yet justified.

Estimation prevents two opposite mistakes. One is building a sharded, multi-region platform for traffic a single server could handle. The other is shipping a design that hits its [bottleneck](node:Bottleneck) in the first week because nobody multiplied the expected users by the payload size.

State every assumption next to its number, because the assumptions are what reviewers can challenge. Plan for peak rather than average traffic, and remember that bits and bytes differ by a factor of eight.
quotes: We'll need Kafka and a dozen nodes for the audit log, right?
Do the back-of-the-envelope estimation first. It's 40 writes per second at peak, and one Postgres instance can handle that.

nodes.name: Latency
nodes.description: The time one operation takes from start to result, usually reported as percentiles because averages hide slow requests.
nodes.markdown:
Latency is the time one operation takes, from the moment it starts to the moment its result arrives. For a web request, that includes network travel, time spent waiting in queues, processing, and the trip back. Some texts reserve "latency" for the waiting part and use "response time" for the total, but in everyday use engineers mean the total.

Latency is reported in percentiles because averages hide the slow requests. The p50 is the median. The p99 is the value that 99% of requests beat. A dashboard can show an 80 ms average while users complain about a slow checkout, because the p99 is 3 seconds. A person who loads many pages per session will run into that slow 1% regularly.

Rough magnitudes are useful for reasoning about where time goes:

| Operation                             | Rough time                       |
| ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Read from main memory                 | About 100 nanoseconds            |
| Random read from an SSD               | Tens to hundreds of microseconds |
| Network round trip in a data centre   | Under 1 millisecond              |
| Network round trip between continents | About 50 to 300 milliseconds     |

These gaps explain many design choices. A [cache](node:Cache) in memory avoids a slower lookup, and a [CDN](node:CDN) moves content closer to the user because no amount of server tuning shortens the distance light travels through fibre.

Latency also depends on load. As a component approaches its capacity, requests spend more time queueing, so latency climbs sharply before [throughput](node:Throughput) reaches its limit. A rising p99 is often the first visible sign of a [bottleneck](node:Bottleneck).

To reduce latency, measure each stage of a request first. Then remove network hops, run independent calls in parallel, or do the work ahead of time.
quotes: The average is fine, so why is support getting complaints about search?
Look at the p99 latency. One request in a hundred takes four seconds, and the average hides it.

nodes.name: Throughput
nodes.description: The amount of work a system completes per unit of time, such as requests per second or messages per minute.
nodes.markdown:
Throughput is the amount of work a system completes per unit of time. It is measured in whatever unit fits the job: requests per second, orders per minute, messages per second, or gigabytes per hour. It counts completed work, so a server that accepts 10,000 requests per second and finishes 6,000 has a throughput of 6,000.

Throughput and [latency](node:Latency) are related but separate. Latency is how long one request takes. Throughput is how many finish per second. A system can have high throughput and poor latency, as a batch job does, or low latency and low throughput, as a single fast worker does.

Little's law connects them. The average number of requests in flight equals throughput multiplied by the average time each one spends in the system:

| Throughput | Average latency | Requests in flight |
| ---------- | --------------- | ------------------ |
| 1,000/s    | 50 ms           | 50                 |
| 1,000/s    | 200 ms          | 200                |
| 1,000/s    | 2 s             | 2,000              |

The table explains a common incident. A database slows from 50 ms to 2 seconds, and at the same arrival rate the number of in-flight requests grows forty-fold. Connection pools and worker threads fill up, and the service starts failing even though traffic did not change.

Every system has a maximum throughput, set by its [bottleneck](node:Bottleneck). As load approaches that limit, requests queue and latency rises. Beyond it, throughput can fall, because the system spends effort on requests that time out before finishing. This is the reason for [load shedding](node:Load%20shedding).

To raise throughput, remove the limiting resource, add capacity with [horizontal scaling](node:Horizontal%20scaling), or batch small operations so each unit of overhead covers more work. Load-test to find the real limit, because a capacity figure derived from one instance rarely holds once instances share a database.
quotes: We doubled the workers, but we still process about 800 jobs a second.
Then workers aren't what limits throughput. Check the database, it's probably saturated.

nodes.name: Bandwidth
nodes.description: The maximum data rate a network link can carry, usually in bits per second. It is a capacity, not the speed you achieve.
nodes.markdown:
Bandwidth is the maximum rate at which a network link can carry data, usually stated in bits per second. A 10 Gbps network card can move at most 10 gigabits each second. It is a capacity. What you actually achieve is [throughput](node:Throughput), which is lower because of protocol overhead, congestion and the speed of whatever sits at each end.

Network capacity is quoted in bits, while file sizes are quoted in bytes, and mixing them up produces estimates that are wrong by a factor of eight. A 1 Gbps link carries at most 125 megabytes per second.

| Link     | Maximum in bytes | Time to move 1 TB at full rate |
| -------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------ |
| 1 Gbps   | 125 MB/s         | About 2.2 hours                |
| 10 Gbps  | 1.25 GB/s        | About 13 minutes               |
| 100 Gbps | 12.5 GB/s        | About 80 seconds               |

Bandwidth and [latency](node:Latency) solve different problems. Bandwidth is the width of the pipe, and latency is how long a byte takes to reach the other end. A larger pipe speeds up a big download but does little for a small API call, whose duration is dominated by round trips. Upgrading a link will not fix a chatty service that makes thirty sequential calls across regions.

Bandwidth becomes the [bottleneck](node:Bottleneck) when payloads are large. A service sending 500 KB images 2,000 times per second needs 1 GB/s, or 8 Gbps, before overhead. On a 10 Gbps card that leaves little headroom, so the service can stall with low CPU and plenty of free memory. When a server looks idle and responses are still slow, check network utilisation.

Common remedies are compressing responses, resizing images, paginating large results, and serving static files from a [CDN](node:CDN). These also reduce data transfer charges, which cloud providers typically bill on outbound traffic.
quotes: CPU is at 20% on the media servers, but downloads crawl at peak.
Check the NICs. We're pushing 9 Gbps through 10 Gbps cards, so we've run out of bandwidth.

nodes.name: Bottleneck
nodes.description: The one resource or component that limits a system's overall throughput, so that improving anything else changes nothing.
nodes.markdown:
A bottleneck is the resource or component that limits how much work a whole system can do. A request path can only move as much work as its most constrained step allows. If the web tier handles 10,000 requests per second and the database handles 2,000, the system's [throughput](node:Throughput) is 2,000.

The usual symptom is that adding capacity has no effect. A team doubles the application servers, and the graphs do not move, because every server is waiting on the same saturated database. In some cases things get worse, since more servers open more connections to the component that is already struggling.

To find a bottleneck, look for the place where work piles up:

| Step | What to check                                                                       |
| ---- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Trace a slow request and see which stage takes the time                             |
| 2    | Check utilisation of CPU, memory, disk and [bandwidth](node:Bandwidth) on each tier |
| 3    | Look for growing queues, full connection pools and lock waits                       |
| 4    | Fix the limiting resource                                                           |
| 5    | Load-test again, because the limit will now sit somewhere else                      |

Step 5 matters because removing one bottleneck exposes the next. Add a [cache](node:Cache) in front of the database and the limit may move to the network or to a single busy partition.

A bottleneck is not always a whole machine. It can be one lock, one [hot key](node:Hot%20key), a single-threaded process using one CPU while the others sit idle, or an external API with a quota. Average utilisation can hide all of these, so inspect individual instances and resources.

Fixes depend on the cause. Options include doing less work per request, adding capacity, splitting the load, or moving slow work to a [message queue](node:Message%20queue) so that it no longer holds up the request.
quotes: We scaled the API to twenty pods and [latency](node:Latency) didn't change.
Then the API isn't the bottleneck. The database has been pinned at 100% CPU since this morning.

nodes.name: Single point of failure
nodes.description: A component whose failure stops the whole system because nothing else can take over its work.
nodes.markdown:
A single point of failure is a component whose failure stops the whole system because nothing else can take over its work. It may be an obvious part, such as the only database server, or a less visible one, such as a single DNS provider, one expiring TLS certificate, or a configuration service every application reads at startup.

The way to remove one is redundancy: run more than one copy, and have a tested way to move work to a surviving copy.

| Component           | Failure without redundancy | Common remedy                                                    |
| ------------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| App server          | Site goes down             | Several instances behind a [load balancer](node:Load%20balancer) |
| Load balancer       | All traffic stops          | Active-passive pair or a managed service                         |
| Primary database    | Writes stop                | Standby copy with automatic failover                             |
| [Cache](node:Cache) | Database takes full load   | Replicated cache, capacity to survive a cold start               |
| Data centre         | Everything in it stops     | Deploy across availability zones (isolated sites)                |

Redundancy only helps if the copies fail independently. Two servers in one rack share a power feed and a network switch. Two services in different zones may both depend on one authentication service. A design diagram can show everything doubled while a shared dependency remains underneath, and teams often discover it during the outage.

Failover also has to work when it is needed. A standby that has silently fallen behind, or a procedure nobody has run in a year, gives false confidence. Test failover on a schedule by actually removing the component.

Removing every single point of failure is rarely worthwhile. Each layer of redundancy adds cost and operational complexity, and the failover machinery can itself fail. Compare the cost of an outage with the cost of the extra copy, using the availability target from your [non-functional requirements](node:Non-functional%20requirement).
quotes: We run three API instances across zones, so we're safe if one goes.
All three read their config from that one Redis box at boot. That's still a single point of failure.

nodes.name: Read-heavy workload
nodes.description: A workload where reads far outnumber writes, which makes caching and read copies effective ways to scale.
nodes.markdown:
A read-heavy workload is one where reads far outnumber writes. Product catalogues, news sites, documentation and social feeds are typical examples, with ratios of 100 reads to one write being common. The ratio matters because reads and writes scale in different ways.

Reads are easier to scale because they do not change anything. The same answer can be copied to many places and served from any of them. The options form a ladder, and each rung adds some complexity:

| Option              | What it does                             | Trade-off                  |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Add indexes         | Lets the database find rows faster       | Slightly slower writes     |
| [Cache](node:Cache) | Serves repeated reads from memory        | Data can be stale          |
| [CDN](node:CDN)     | Serves content from locations near users | Harder to purge            |
| Read replicas       | Database copies that answer read queries | Copies can lag the primary |
| Precomputed views   | Stores the finished answer ahead of time | Extra work on each write   |

The usual symptom of an unaddressed read-heavy workload is a database at high CPU while running the same few queries thousands of times per second. A [cache-aside](node:Cache-aside) layer often removes most of that load.

The price of these techniques is staleness. A read replica applies changes shortly after the primary, so a user can save a profile, reload and see the old value because the second request hit a copy that has not caught up. For that case, send a user's reads to the primary for a short period after they write, or read that user's own data from the primary.

Measure the ratio before relying on it. Some workloads that look read-heavy have write bursts, and a [write-heavy workload](node:Write-heavy%20workload) calls for different techniques.
quotes: The catalogue database is at 90% CPU, should we shard it?
It's a read-heavy workload with about a thousand reads per write. Put a cache in front before splitting anything.

nodes.name: Write-heavy workload
nodes.description: A workload dominated by incoming writes, such as logs or sensor data, where caches and read copies give little relief.
nodes.markdown:
A write-heavy workload is one where a large share of the traffic creates or changes data. Metrics collection, application logs, sensor readings, click tracking and chat messages are typical examples.

Writes are harder to scale than reads because each one must reach durable storage and stay correct. A [cache](node:Cache) does little to absorb them. Read replicas (database copies that serve queries) do not help either, because every replica has to apply every write, and heavy write load can make those copies fall behind.

The symptoms differ from a read problem. Disk I/O saturates, lock waits climb, replicas lag by minutes, and insert [latency](node:Latency) grows as tables and their indexes get larger. Each index adds work to every insert, so a table with many indexes can be slow to write even when its queries are fast.

| Technique                             | How it helps                                | Trade-off                       |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Batching                              | Groups many rows into one write             | Small delay, larger loss window |
| Fewer indexes                         | Reduces work per insert                     | Some queries get slower         |
| [Message queue](node:Message%20queue) | Absorbs bursts ahead of the database        | Data is visible later           |
| Write-optimised storage               | Appends to disk and merges later (LSM tree) | Reads can cost more             |
| Partitioning                          | Splits writes across several machines       | Harder queries, rebalancing     |

Partitioning needs a well-chosen key. If all writes for the current hour land on one partition, as happens when data is range-partitioned by timestamp, one machine takes the entire load. This hot partition has the same effect as a [hot key](node:Hot%20key). Mixing in a device or user ID spreads the writes.

Check whether every write needs the same guarantee. Losing one click event may be acceptable, while losing a payment is not. Data you can afford to lose can use batching or a [write-behind cache](node:Write-behind%20cache).
quotes: Replica lag hits ten minutes whenever the sensors report.
It's a write-heavy workload. More replicas won't help, so batch the inserts and drop the indexes nobody uses.

nodes.name: Vertical scaling
nodes.description: Handling more load by giving one machine more CPU, memory or faster storage, also called scaling up.
nodes.markdown:
Vertical scaling means handling more load by giving one machine more resources: more CPU cores, more memory, faster disks or a faster network card. It is also called scaling up. On a cloud provider it can be as small a change as selecting a larger instance type.

The main advantage is that the software usually does not change. There is no data to split, no coordination between machines, and no new failure modes from network calls. For databases in particular, moving to a larger machine is often the sensible first step, because the alternative of splitting data across servers adds lasting complexity.

Vertical scaling has limits that eventually force a different approach:

| Limit            | What happens                                                                               |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Hardware ceiling | There is a largest machine you can buy or rent                                             |
| Cost curve       | The largest machines can cost more per unit of capacity                                    |
| Resize downtime  | Moving to a larger machine often requires a restart                                        |
| Availability     | One large machine is still a [single point of failure](node:Single%20point%20of%20failure) |
| Software limits  | Locks or single-threaded code may not use the added cores                                  |

The last limit is a common surprise. A team moves a service to a 64-core machine and sees no improvement, because one thread is pinned at 100% while the rest sit idle. Before resizing, confirm which resource is the [bottleneck](node:Bottleneck). More cores do nothing for a service limited by a lock, and more memory does nothing for one limited by disk writes.

Most production systems combine both directions: [stateless](node:Stateless%20service) application servers grow through [horizontal scaling](node:Horizontal%20scaling), while the database grows vertically for as long as that remains practical.
quotes: Do we need to shard the orders database this quarter?
Not yet. Vertical scaling buys us a year or so. Move it to the next instance size and revisit when we're near the top of the range.

nodes.name: Horizontal scaling
nodes.description: Handling more load by adding more machines and spreading work across them, also called scaling out.
nodes.markdown:
Horizontal scaling means handling more load by adding more machines and spreading the work across them. It is also called scaling out. Instead of one larger server, you run ten ordinary ones behind a [load balancer](node:Load%20balancer), and add an eleventh when traffic grows.

The comparison with [vertical scaling](node:Vertical%20scaling) is mostly a trade of simplicity for headroom:

| Concern         | Vertical                  | Horizontal                              |
| --------------- | ------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Capacity limit  | Largest available machine | Much higher, depends on the design      |
| Code changes    | Usually none              | Must tolerate several running copies    |
| Machine failure | Full outage               | Lose a fraction of capacity             |
| Deploys         | Restart causes downtime   | Replace instances one at a time         |
| Operations      | One machine to manage     | Networking, discovery, partial failures |

Horizontal scaling works well for a [stateless service](node:Stateless%20service), because any instance can answer any request. State is what makes it hard. If each server keeps sessions in its own memory, a user's next request can land on a server that has never seen them. Databases are harder still, since spreading writes means sharding (splitting data across machines by a key), which complicates queries and transactions.

A common disappointment is adding servers and getting no improvement. If every instance waits on one database, that database is the [bottleneck](node:Bottleneck), and extra instances add connections to it. Scaling only helps the part that is actually constrained.

Costs also appear between machines. A process that kept a counter in memory now has several disagreeing counters, and a scheduled job runs once per instance unless something coordinates it. Check for assumptions like these before scaling a service that has only ever run as one copy.
quotes: Traffic doubles for the sale, can we add API pods?
Yes, the API scales horizontally. The checkout worker doesn't, because it keeps a lock in memory, so fix that before relying on horizontal scaling there.

nodes.name: Stateless service
nodes.description: A service that keeps no client data in its own memory between requests, so any instance can handle any request.
nodes.markdown:
A stateless service keeps no client-specific data in its own memory or disk between requests. Everything needed to answer arrives with the request or is fetched from a shared store such as a database. Because of this, any running instance can handle any request.

The state still exists. It has moved out of the application process into something built to hold it:

| State             | Stateful version         | Stateless version                                             |
| ----------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Login session     | Object in server memory  | Shared session store or signed token                          |
| Shopping cart     | Variable on one instance | Database row keyed by user                                    |
| Uploaded file     | Local disk               | Object storage                                                |
| Progress of a job | In-process loop          | Record in a [message queue](node:Message%20queue) or database |

The symptom of hidden state is behaviour that depends on which server you reach. Users get logged out at random, a file uploaded a moment ago returns a 404 on refresh, or everything breaks right after a deploy because the restart wiped memory. These faults often appear only once a second instance is added, since a single server hides the problem.

Statelessness is what makes [horizontal scaling](node:Horizontal%20scaling) straightforward. A [load balancer](node:Load%20balancer) can send traffic anywhere, instances can be replaced during a deploy, and a crashed instance loses only the requests it was processing at that moment. Without it, teams often resort to a [sticky session](node:Sticky%20session), which keeps the problem and adds new ones.

An in-process [cache](node:Cache) does not break the model, provided losing it affects only speed. The test is whether an instance can be killed at any moment with no lasting effect on users.

The cost is that each request may need a trip to the shared store, which adds [latency](node:Latency) and makes that store a dependency of every request.
quotes: Why do people lose their carts every time we deploy?
The cart lives in process memory, so this isn't a stateless service. Move it to Redis and restarts stop mattering.

nodes.name: Sticky session
nodes.description: A load balancer setting that keeps sending one client to the same server, usually because that server holds its session.
nodes.markdown:
A sticky session is a [load balancer](node:Load%20balancer) setting that keeps sending the same client to the same backend server. It is also called session affinity. It is typically used when a server holds something about that client in local memory, such as a login session, and other servers could not answer without it.

There are two common ways to implement it:

| Method    | How the client is identified                    | Weakness                                                             |
| --------- | ----------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Cookie    | Balancer sets or reads a cookie naming a server | Requires [layer 7 load balancing](node:Layer%207%20load%20balancing) |
| Source IP | Balancer hashes the client's IP address         | Many users behind one office or mobile network share an IP           |

Stickiness makes a stateful application run on several servers with little code change, which is why it is often adopted. The costs show up later. Load becomes uneven, because a few heavy users stay pinned to one instance while others idle. Adding servers does not relieve the busy ones right away, since existing clients stay where they are.

Failure is the most visible problem. When a server crashes or is replaced during a deploy, every user pinned to it loses their session, and people find themselves logged out or with an empty form. Rolling deploys become slower too, because you must either wait for sessions to drain from an instance or accept that those users lose them.

The usual fix is to make the application a [stateless service](node:Stateless%20service) by moving session data to a shared store, or into a signed token held by the client. Stickiness can then be removed.

It still has legitimate uses as an optimisation. Routing a user back to a server with a warm local [cache](node:Cache) improves speed, and the system still works correctly if the routing changes.
quotes: Why are a third of users logged out after each deploy?
We use sticky sessions and keep the session in memory, so restarting a pod logs out everyone pinned to it.

nodes.name: Consistent hashing
nodes.description: A way of assigning keys to servers so that adding or removing a server moves only a small share of the keys.
nodes.markdown:
Consistent hashing is a way of assigning keys to servers so that adding or removing a server moves only a small share of the keys. It is used in distributed [caches](node:Cache) and partitioned data stores, where each key must live on a predictable node.

The simpler approach is `hash(key) % N`, where N is the number of servers. It spreads keys evenly, but changing N changes the result for nearly every key. Going from 4 servers to 5 sends about 80% of keys to a different server. In a cache, that shows up as a sudden collapse in [cache hit ratio](node:Cache%20hit%20ratio) right after someone adds a node, with the database taking the resulting load.

Consistent hashing avoids this by placing both servers and keys on the same circular range of hash values:

| Step | What happens                                         |
| ---- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Hash each server's name to a position on the ring    |
| 2    | Hash the key to a position on the same ring          |
| 3    | Walk clockwise from the key until you reach a server |
| 4    | That server owns the key                             |

When a server joins, it takes over only the keys between itself and the previous server on the ring. When one leaves, its keys pass to the next server. Going from 4 to 5 servers moves about 20% of keys.

With a few servers placed at random positions, some arcs of the ring are much longer than others, so load is uneven. The standard fix is virtual nodes: each physical server appears at many positions on the ring. A larger machine can be given more positions.

Consistent hashing balances the number of keys and does nothing about uneven popularity. A single [hot key](node:Hot%20key) still lands on one server and can overload it.
quotes: Every time we add a Redis node, the database gets hammered for ten minutes.
The client is doing modulo hashing, so nearly every key remaps. Switch it to consistent hashing.

nodes.name: Fan-out
nodes.description: One request or message that triggers many downstream calls or copies. The number of targets is the fan-out factor.
nodes.markdown:
Fan-out is when one incoming request or message triggers many downstream calls or copies. A search query sent to 50 index partitions has a fan-out of 50. A post delivered to 10,000 followers has a fan-out of 10,000. The term appears in two main settings.

| Setting         | What multiplies                     | Typical example                      |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Request fan-out | Synchronous calls to other services | A page calling 12 services to render |
| Data fan-out    | Copies of a message or record       | One event delivered to many inboxes  |

Request fan-out has a counter-intuitive effect on [latency](node:Latency). If a request must wait for all its downstream calls, it is as slow as the slowest one, so rare slowness becomes common. Suppose each backend exceeds one second on 1% of calls. A request that calls 100 of them in parallel has a 1 − 0.99¹⁰⁰ chance, about 63%, of hitting at least one slow response. This is why a page can feel slow when every service's dashboard looks healthy.

Several techniques reduce the effect. Call backends in parallel, give each call a [timeout](node:Timeout), and return partial results when an optional backend is late, which is a form of [graceful degradation](node:Graceful%20degradation). A hedged request sends a duplicate to another replica if the first has not answered after a short delay, and uses whichever reply comes first.

Fan-out also multiplies load. One user action becoming 100 internal calls means a modest traffic increase can overload deep dependencies, and any [retries](node:Retry%20with%20backoff) multiply it again.

Data fan-out raises a timing question: do the copying when content is written, or assemble it when someone reads? Those two designs are [fan-out on write](node:Fan-out%20on%20write) and [fan-out on read](node:Fan-out%20on%20read).
quotes: Every service is under 100 ms at p99, but the dashboard page takes three seconds.
It has a fan-out of about 40 calls, partly in sequence. The slow ones add up.

nodes.name: Fan-out on write
nodes.description: Copying new content to every recipient's feed when it is created, so that later reads are fast and already prepared.
nodes.markdown:
[Fan-out](node:Fan-out) on write means copying new content to every recipient's feed at the moment it is created. Each user has a precomputed timeline, usually a list of post IDs in a fast store, and reading it is one lookup. It is one of two ways to build a feed, the other being [fan-out on read](node:Fan-out%20on%20read). Both are forms of data fan-out.

The write path usually runs in the background:

| Step | Who     | What happens                                                                              |
| ---- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | API     | Saves the post                                                                            |
| 2    | API     | Puts a job on a [message queue](node:Message%20queue), then returns success to the author |
| 3    | Worker  | Looks up the author's followers                                                           |
| 4    | Workers | Insert the post ID into each follower's stored timeline                                   |
| 5    | Reader  | Fetches their timeline with a single read                                                 |

This suits a [read-heavy workload](node:Read-heavy%20workload). The expensive work happens once per post, and the many reads that follow are inexpensive and predictable.

The weakness is accounts with very large audiences. One post from an account with 20 million followers creates 20 million timeline writes. The queue backs up, and followers see that post minutes late, while posts from smaller accounts queued behind it are delayed too.

Storage grows as well, since the same post ID is stored once per follower. Systems limit this by keeping only the most recent few hundred entries per timeline and by skipping inactive users. Edits and deletes are also harder, because removing a post means finding every copy, or filtering deleted posts at read time.

Large systems commonly use a hybrid. Ordinary accounts fan out on write, while posts from very large accounts are fetched and merged when a follower reads.
quotes: Why did the feed queue spike to two million jobs at noon?
A celebrity account posted. With fan-out on write, that's one job per follower, so we should exclude big accounts and merge them at read time.

nodes.name: Fan-out on read
nodes.description: Assembling a user's feed at the moment they request it, by fetching and merging recent content from each source.
nodes.markdown:
[Fan-out](node:Fan-out) on read means assembling a user's feed at the moment they request it. Nothing is prepared in advance. When a user opens the app, the service looks up who they follow, fetches recent posts from each account, merges them by time or rank, and returns the result. It is also called the pull model, in contrast to [fan-out on write](node:Fan-out%20on%20write), the push model.

| Concern                      | Fan-out on write           | Fan-out on read          |
| ---------------------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Cost of posting              | High, grows with followers | Low, one insert          |
| Cost of reading              | Low, one lookup            | High, grows with follows |
| Read [latency](node:Latency) | Low and steady             | Higher and more variable |
| Storage                      | One copy per follower      | One copy of each post    |
| Freshness                    | Delayed by the queue       | Current at read time     |
| Inactive users               | Work wasted on them        | Cost nothing             |
| Very large accounts          | Expensive to post          | No extra cost            |

Fan-out on read suits data that is written often and read rarely, and products where most users are inactive on a given day. Deleting a post also takes effect immediately, since no copies exist.

The symptom of this design under load is a slow home screen for the most connected users. Someone who follows 5,000 accounts triggers 5,000 lookups, or a large query across many partitions, every time they refresh. Because the request waits on many sources, it is exposed to the tail-latency effect of fan-out, where one slow partition delays the whole response.

Common mitigations are to [cache](node:Cache) the assembled feed for a short time, cap how many sources are read per request, and fetch only the first page. Many large products combine the two approaches: precompute timelines for ordinary accounts, and pull posts from very large accounts during the read.
quotes: Should we precompute notifications for every workspace member?
Most members never open that tab. Use fan-out on read and cache the result for a minute.

nodes.name: Hot key
nodes.description: One key that receives far more traffic than others, overloading the single node that stores it while the rest sit idle.
nodes.markdown:
A hot key is a single key that receives far more traffic than the others, overloading the node that stores it. In a partitioned [cache](node:Cache) or database, each key lives on one node or a small set of nodes, so a viral product page or a very popular account sends its traffic to one place regardless of how large the cluster is.

The recognisable symptom is one node at 100% CPU while the others sit at 15%. Cluster-wide averages look healthy, more nodes do not help, and requests touching unrelated keys on the same node also slow down. [Consistent hashing](node:Consistent%20hashing) does not prevent this, because it balances how many keys each node owns and takes no account of how popular each key is.

Hot keys are found by sampling per-key traffic. Redis, for example, offers `redis-cli --hotkeys` when an LFU [eviction policy](node:Eviction%20policy) is configured.

The fix depends on whether the traffic is reads or writes:

| Technique              | Works for | How it helps                                              |
| ---------------------- | --------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Local in-process cache | Reads     | Each app server keeps the value for a second or two       |
| Replicate the key      | Reads     | Several nodes hold copies and share the requests          |
| Key splitting          | Reads     | Store copies as `item:1`, `item:2` and pick one at random |
| Counter splitting      | Writes    | Increment one of N sub-counters and sum them on read      |
| Write batching         | Writes    | Combine many updates in the app before writing            |
| Dedicated node         | Both      | Move the key to hardware of its own                       |

A one-second local cache limits each app server to about one fetch per second for that key.

A hot key that expires is a further risk. Every request misses simultaneously and goes to the database, producing a [cache stampede](node:Cache%20stampede).
quotes: Redis shard 7 is maxed out and the other eleven are idle.
That's a hot key, probably the homepage banner. Add a short local cache in the app.

nodes.name: Load balancer
nodes.description: A component that spreads incoming requests across a group of servers and stops sending traffic to unhealthy ones.
nodes.markdown:
A load balancer is a component that receives incoming requests and spreads them across a group of backend servers. Clients see one address, while several instances do the work. This is what makes [horizontal scaling](node:Horizontal%20scaling) possible for a web service, and it lets you replace instances during a deploy without clients noticing.

The balancer chooses a backend using an algorithm:

| Algorithm            | How it picks                               | Suits                                |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------ |
| Round robin          | Each server in turn                        | Similar servers, similar requests    |
| Weighted round robin | In turn, in proportion to assigned weights | Servers of different sizes           |
| Least connections    | Server with the fewest active connections  | Requests of varying duration         |
| Hash                 | Same client or key goes to the same server | Affinity, local [caches](node:Cache) |
| Power of two choices | Samples two at random, takes the less busy | Large fleets, several balancers      |

Balancers operate at different levels. [Layer 4 load balancing](node:Layer%204%20load%20balancing) routes network connections without reading their content, while [layer 7 load balancing](node:Layer%207%20load%20balancing) reads each HTTP request and can route on its path or headers.

Health checks decide which instances receive traffic, and they cause two familiar problems. A shallow check that only confirms the process is running can keep returning 200 while real requests fail, so users keep hitting a broken instance. A deep check that also tests the shared database has the opposite risk: one database blip marks every instance unhealthy at once, and the balancer may have nowhere to send traffic. A common compromise is to check what the instance itself needs to function and handle shared dependency failures separately.

The balancer sits on every request, so it can become a [single point of failure](node:Single%20point%20of%20failure). Run it as a redundant pair or use a managed service.
quotes: Why are 25% of requests failing when only one of four pods is broken?
Its health endpoint still returns 200, so the load balancer keeps sending it traffic.

nodes.name: Layer 4 load balancing
nodes.description: Distributing network connections using only IP addresses and ports, without reading the data inside them.
nodes.markdown:
Layer 4 load balancing distributes network connections using only IP addresses, ports and the protocol, without reading the data inside them. The name comes from the transport layer, layer 4 of the OSI networking model, which is where TCP and UDP sit. The [load balancer](node:Load%20balancer) picks a backend when a connection opens, and every packet in that connection then goes to the same backend.

Not parsing the content has these consequences:

| Property                           | Consequence                                    |
| ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| No parsing of application data     | Low overhead per connection                    |
| Works with any TCP or UDP protocol | Suits databases, message brokers, game traffic |
| Encrypted traffic passes through   | TLS can stay end-to-end, up to the backend     |
| Sees no URL, header or cookie      | Cannot route by path or user                   |
| Decides once per connection        | Balances connections, not requests             |

The last property causes a well-known problem with long-lived connections. HTTP/2 and gRPC (a remote procedure call framework) send many requests over one connection. A layer 4 balancer sees one connection and pins it to one backend, so a busy client can load one server heavily while others sit idle.

The same effect shows up during scaling. You add three new pods, and they receive almost no traffic, because existing clients keep their open connections to the old pods.

There are three usual fixes. Set a maximum connection age so clients reconnect and spread out over time. Use client-side balancing, where the client holds connections to several backends. Or move to [layer 7 load balancing](node:Layer%207%20load%20balancing), which balances each request individually.

Layer 4 remains a good fit for non-HTTP protocols and very high connection counts. AWS Network Load Balancer and HAProxy in TCP mode are examples.
quotes: We scaled gRPC to ten pods, but three of them are doing all the work.
The service is behind layer 4 load balancing, so each connection is stuck to one pod. Set a max connection age.

nodes.name: Layer 7 load balancing
nodes.description: Distributing individual requests by reading application data such as the URL path, headers and cookies.
nodes.markdown:
Layer 7 load balancing distributes individual requests by reading application data such as the URL path, headers and cookies. The name refers to the application layer of the OSI networking model, where HTTP sits. The [load balancer](node:Load%20balancer) ends the client's connection, reads the request, chooses a backend, and sends the request over its own connection. In this role it is a type of [reverse proxy](node:Reverse%20proxy).

Reading the request allows routing rules that lower layers cannot express. `/api/*` can go to one service and `/images/*` to another, a header can send 5% of users to a canary release (a small trial deployment), and a cookie can support a [sticky session](node:Sticky%20session).

| Concern                       | [Layer 4](node:Layer%204%20load%20balancing) | Layer 7                          |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Routes on                     | IP address and port                          | Path, host, headers, cookies     |
| Balances                      | Connections                                  | Individual requests              |
| Protocols                     | Any TCP or UDP                               | Those it can parse, such as HTTP |
| TLS                           | Can pass through                             | Usually terminated here          |
| Overhead                      | Lower                                        | Higher                           |
| Request retries, header edits | Not available                                | Supported                        |

The cost is more work per request. The balancer must decrypt traffic, parse it and hold state for two connections, and it needs access to your TLS private keys. It also adds its own limits, which produce confusing failures. A file upload that works locally returns 413 in production because of a body-size limit on the balancer. A long report returns 504 because the balancer's [timeout](node:Timeout) is shorter than the application's. When an error never appears in your application logs, check the balancer's logs.

Automatic retries at this layer need care. Retrying a failed POST can apply it twice unless the operation is idempotent, meaning repeating it has the same effect as doing it once.

NGINX, Envoy and AWS Application Load Balancer are common examples.
quotes: Can we send only `/search` traffic to the new service?
Yes, the ingress does layer 7 load balancing, so it's one path rule.

nodes.name: Reverse proxy
nodes.description: A server that sits in front of backend servers, receives client requests on their behalf, and forwards them.
nodes.markdown:
A reverse proxy is a server that sits in front of one or more backend servers, receives client requests on their behalf, and forwards them. The client talks only to the proxy and usually cannot tell what is behind it. A forward proxy is the mirror image: it acts for clients, for example a company proxy that controls outbound web access.

Putting one component at the entrance lets it handle work that every backend would otherwise repeat:

| Job                   | What the proxy does                                                 |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| TLS termination       | Handles HTTPS so backends can receive decrypted traffic             |
| Routing               | Sends paths or hostnames to different services                      |
| Balancing             | Spreads requests, acting as a [load balancer](node:Load%20balancer) |
| [Caching](node:Cache) | Stores responses and serves repeats                                 |
| Compression           | Shrinks responses before sending them                               |
| Buffering             | Absorbs slow clients so backend workers are freed quickly           |
| Static files          | Serves assets without involving the application                     |

The proxy also introduces a class of errors that can confuse debugging. A 502 Bad Gateway means the proxy got an invalid response or no usable connection from the backend, often because the application crashed or is not listening. A 504 Gateway [Timeout](node:Timeout) means the backend did not answer within the proxy's time limit. In both cases the error page comes from the proxy, so the application's logs may show nothing, or show a request that completed successfully after the proxy gave up.

Another common surprise is that every request appears to come from the proxy's IP address. Proxies pass the original address in a header such as `X-Forwarded-For`. Clients can forge that header, so trust only the values added by your own proxies, particularly for [rate limiting](node:Rate%20limiting) and audit logs.

NGINX, HAProxy, Caddy and Envoy are examples. An [API gateway](node:API%20gateway) is a reverse proxy with API-specific features added.
quotes: Users get a 502, but there's nothing in the app logs.
The reverse proxy generates that. The app probably crashed and restarted, so check for container restarts.

nodes.name: API gateway
nodes.description: A single entry point for API clients that handles routing, authentication, rate limits and other shared request concerns.
nodes.markdown:
An API gateway is a single entry point for API clients that routes each request to the right backend service and handles concerns shared by all of them. It is a specialised [reverse proxy](node:Reverse%20proxy). It is common in [microservices](node:Microservices), where clients would otherwise need to know the address and rules of many separate services.

Without one, each service reimplements login checks and limits, usually with small differences. One team's endpoint ends up with weaker validation, or a security fix has to ship in twelve places. A gateway puts those rules in one layer.

| Concern                               | What the gateway does                          |
| ------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Routing                               | Maps public paths to internal services         |
| Authentication                        | Validates tokens or API keys before forwarding |
| [Rate limiting](node:Rate%20limiting) | Enforces quotas per client or plan             |
| Transformation                        | Rewrites headers, paths or payload formats     |
| Versioning                            | Sends `/v1` and `/v2` to different backends    |
| Observability                         | Records logs and metrics for every call        |

The neighbouring components overlap. A [load balancer](node:Load%20balancer) spreads traffic across copies of one service. A reverse proxy forwards traffic and handles generic HTTP work. An API gateway adds knowledge of API consumers, such as who is calling and what plan they are on.

The main risk is logic creep. Teams add business rules, data joins and special cases to the gateway because it is convenient, and it becomes a shared component that every release depends on and one team must approve. Keep rules about the product inside services, and keep the gateway to cross-cutting concerns. If different clients need different response shapes, a [backend for frontend](node:Backend%20for%20frontend) is a better location.

The gateway also adds a network hop and sits on every request, so a bad configuration change can take down all APIs at once. Kong and Amazon API Gateway are examples.
quotes: Should the discount calculation go in a gateway plugin? It's the one place every request passes through.
No, that's business logic. Keep the API gateway to auth, routing and quotas.

nodes.name: CDN
nodes.description: A content delivery network, a set of servers in many locations that cache content close to users.
nodes.markdown:
A CDN, or content delivery network, is a set of servers in many geographic locations that [cache](node:Cache) content close to users. Those servers are called the edge. Your own server is called the origin. A user in Tokyo can get an image from a nearby edge location instead of an origin in Virginia, which lowers [latency](node:Latency) and origin load.

A request moves through these steps:

| Step | Who     | What happens                                                      |
| ---- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Network | DNS or network routing sends the user to a nearby edge location   |
| 2    | Edge    | Looks up the response by its cache key, usually the URL           |
| 3    | Edge    | On a hit, returns the stored copy                                 |
| 4    | Origin  | On a miss, receives the request and returns the response          |
| 5    | Edge    | Stores it according to its `Cache-Control` headers, then responds |

CDNs suit images, video, scripts and stylesheets, and can also cache API responses that are the same for many users.

The familiar failure is stale content. You deploy a fix and some users still get the old stylesheet, because edge locations hold it until its [TTL](node:TTL) expires. Purging helps but takes time to reach every location and does not clear browser caches. A more dependable method is to put a content hash in the filename, such as `app.3f9c2.css`. Each release then has a new URL, and the file can be cached for a long time.

A more serious failure is caching personalised content. If an account page is cached under a URL shared by all users, one person can receive another's data. Mark such responses `Cache-Control: private` or `no-store`, and make sure the cache key includes anything the response varies on.

Cloudflare, Amazon CloudFront and Fastly are examples.
quotes: I shipped the CSS fix an hour ago, but customers still see the broken layout.
The CDN is still serving the old file. We need hashed filenames so each release gets a new URL.

nodes.name: Service discovery
nodes.description: The mechanism services use to find the current network addresses of the other services they call.
nodes.markdown:
Service discovery is the mechanism services use to find the current network addresses of the services they call. Hard-coded addresses stop working once instances are created and destroyed by autoscaling and deploys, because each new instance can have a different IP. A discovery system maintains a live list of healthy instances under a stable service name, such as `payments`.

The list lives in a registry. Instances either register themselves on startup or are registered by the platform, and health checks remove those that stop responding. Callers then reach an instance in one of three ways:

| Approach    | How a caller finds an instance                                            | Trade-off                                                         |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| DNS-based   | Resolves the service name to one or more IPs                              | Simple, but resolvers and clients [cache](node:Cache) old records |
| Client-side | Fetches the list from the registry and picks an instance itself           | No extra hop, but logic in every client                           |
| Server-side | Calls a stable address, and a [load balancer](node:Load%20balancer) picks | Simple clients, one more hop                                      |

Kubernetes Services and Consul are examples.

The usual symptom of a discovery problem is a burst of connection errors during every deploy. An old pod has shut down, but callers still hold its address for a few seconds, or longer if a client caches DNS results for too long and ignores the record's [TTL](node:TTL). To reduce this, have an instance leave the registry first, keep serving during a short draining period, and only then exit. Callers should also retry a failed connection on a different instance.

The registry becomes a dependency of nearly everything, so an outage there can spread widely. Run it with redundancy, and have clients keep using their last known list of addresses if the registry cannot be reached.
quotes: Every rollout gives us thirty seconds of connection refused from the orders service.
Pods exit before service discovery removes them. Add a pre-stop delay so they drain first.

nodes.name: Rate limiting
nodes.description: Capping how many requests a client can make in a period of time and rejecting the excess, usually with HTTP 429.
nodes.markdown:
Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a period of time and rejects the excess. A rule might allow 100 requests per minute per API key. It protects a service from abusive clients, buggy scripts stuck in a loop, and one tenant using capacity that others need. Rejected HTTP requests normally receive a 429 Too Many Requests status, often with a `Retry-After` header saying when to try again.

Several algorithms can enforce the limit:

| Algorithm                                                 | How it counts                      | Trade-off                         |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Fixed window                                              | Counter per calendar minute        | Allows a double burst at the edge |
| Sliding log                                               | Stores a timestamp per request     | Exact, but uses more memory       |
| [Sliding window counter](node:Sliding%20window%20counter) | Weights two adjacent counters      | Approximate, low memory           |
| [Token bucket](node:Token%20bucket)                       | Spends tokens that refill steadily | Permits controlled bursts         |
| Leaky bucket                                              | Drains a queue at a fixed rate     | Smooth output, adds waiting       |

Identifying the client needs thought. Limiting by IP address punishes everyone behind one office network or mobile carrier, so a whole company can receive 429s because of one colleague's script. Prefer an API key or user ID, and keep IP limits for unauthenticated endpoints such as login.

Running several instances introduces a common bug. If each instance counts on its own, a limit of 100 per minute across three instances really allows 300. A shared store such as Redis fixes this, provided the check and increment happen atomically. You also need to decide what happens when that store is down: allow traffic and lose protection, or reject it and cause an outage.

Rate limiting differs from [load shedding](node:Load%20shedding). Rate limiting enforces a per-client quota even when the system is healthy, while load shedding drops work because the system as a whole is overloaded.
quotes: A partner's sync job is eating half of our API capacity.
Add rate limiting per API key and return `Retry-After`, so their client backs off.

nodes.name: Token bucket
nodes.description: A rate limiting algorithm where requests spend tokens that refill at a steady rate, allowing short bursts up to a set size.
nodes.markdown:
A token bucket is a [rate limiting](node:Rate%20limiting) algorithm in which each request spends a token from a bucket that refills at a steady rate. It has two settings: capacity, the most tokens the bucket can hold, and refill rate, how many tokens are added per second. Capacity controls the size of a burst, and refill rate controls the sustained average.

Take a bucket with a capacity of 20 and a refill rate of 5 tokens per second:

| Time | Event                | Tokens after | Result                |
| ---- | -------------------- | ------------ | --------------------- |
| 0 s  | Client has been idle | 20           | Bucket is full        |
| 0 s  | 20 requests arrive   | 0            | All allowed           |
| 0 s  | 1 more request       | 0            | Rejected              |
| 1 s  | 5 tokens added       | 5            | Refilled              |
| 1 s  | 8 requests arrive    | 0            | 5 allowed, 3 rejected |

This burst behaviour suits real clients. A page load may fire ten API calls at once and then go quiet. A strict per-second limit would reject part of that page even though the user's average rate is low. A token bucket lets it through and still holds the long-run rate.

Implementations do not need a timer adding tokens. Store only the token count and the last update time. On each request, compute `tokens = min(capacity, tokens + elapsed × rate)`, then subtract one if at least one token is available. Across several servers, this read-and-update has to be atomic, for example through a Lua script in Redis. Otherwise two concurrent requests can spend the same token.

Choosing the capacity is the main tuning decision. If it is too small, normal bursts receive 429 errors even though the client is under its average limit. If it is too large, many clients can burst together and still overload the backend.
quotes: Customers get 429s on dashboard load, but they're well under 300 requests a minute.
The page sends 40 calls at once. Use a token bucket with a burst capacity of 50.

nodes.name: Sliding window counter
nodes.description: A rate limiting algorithm that estimates recent traffic by weighting the counts of the current and previous time windows.
nodes.markdown:
A sliding window counter is a [rate limiting](node:Rate%20limiting) algorithm that estimates recent traffic by combining the counts of the current and previous fixed time windows. It uses about as little memory as a plain counter and reduces that counter's main flaw.

The flaw is the boundary burst. A fixed window limit of 100 requests per minute resets at the top of each minute. A client can send 100 requests at 12:00:59 and another 100 at 12:01:00. Each window is within its limit, yet the backend receives 200 requests in about one second, double the intended rate.

The sliding window counter keeps two numbers per client and weights the older one by how much of it still overlaps the last 60 seconds:

| Step | Calculation                             | Example             |
| ---- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| 1    | Count in the previous window            | 80                  |
| 2    | Count so far in the current window      | 30                  |
| 3    | Position in the current window          | 15 s of 60 s        |
| 4    | Share of previous window still in range | 1 − 15/60 = 75%     |
| 5    | Estimate = previous × share + current   | 80 × 0.75 + 30 = 90 |
| 6    | Compare with the limit of 100           | Allowed             |

The estimate assumes requests in the previous window were spread evenly. When they were bunched at one end, the estimate can be far off: a client can fit nearly twice the limit into a rolling window, or is rejected after a minute of sending nothing. On evenly spread traffic the error is small. For quotas and abuse protection that error is normally acceptable. A sliding log is exact, at a higher memory cost.

Compared with a [token bucket](node:Token%20bucket), this algorithm expresses a limit directly as "N per window" and does not grant an explicit burst allowance.
quotes: Clients are doubling their quota by bursting right around the minute mark.
That's the fixed window edge. Switch to a sliding window counter, which only needs one extra integer per client.

nodes.name: Cache
nodes.description: A fast store holding copies of data so that repeated requests can avoid a slower source such as a database.
nodes.markdown:
A cache is a fast store that holds copies of data so that repeated requests can avoid a slower source, such as a database, a disk or a remote service. When the requested item is present, that is a hit. When it is absent, that is a miss, and the data must be fetched from the source. Caching works because access is usually uneven, with a small share of the data receiving a large share of the requests.

Caches exist at several levels of a typical system:

| Level                                 | Where it lives            | Typical contents             |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Browser                               | User's device             | Images, scripts, stylesheets |
| [CDN](node:CDN)                       | Edge locations near users | Static files, public pages   |
| [Reverse proxy](node:Reverse%20proxy) | In front of app servers   | Whole HTTP responses         |
| In-process                            | Application memory        | Config, small lookup tables  |
| Distributed                           | Redis or Memcached        | Sessions, query results      |
| Database                              | Database memory           | Recently used data pages     |

Every cache design answers three questions. How does data get in, for example [cache-aside](node:Cache-aside) or a [write-through cache](node:Write-through%20cache)? How long does it stay, as set by a [TTL](node:TTL) and an [eviction policy](node:Eviction%20policy)? How is it corrected when the source changes, which is [cache invalidation](node:Cache%20invalidation)?

Two failures are common. The first is stale data: a user changes their address, and the old one keeps appearing because a cached copy outlived the change. The second is hidden dependence. A database is sized for the traffic left over after the cache, so when the cache restarts empty, the database receives the full load in a [cache stampede](node:Cache%20stampede) and can go down. A cache that was added to improve speed has become necessary for availability.

Treat a cache as a copy that can vanish at any time, and track its [cache hit ratio](node:Cache%20hit%20ratio). Test what happens when it is empty.
quotes: Can we restart the Redis cluster during the day?
Not safely. The cache absorbs about 95% of reads, and the database can't take that load cold.

nodes.name: Cache hit ratio
nodes.description: The share of lookups a cache answers without going to the source, calculated as hits divided by total lookups.
nodes.markdown:
[Cache](node:Cache) hit ratio is the share of lookups that a cache answers without going to the underlying source. It is calculated as hits divided by hits plus misses. A cache that answers 950 of 1,000 lookups has a hit ratio of 95%.

The number that matters for capacity is the miss ratio, because misses are what reach the database. Small changes near the top of the scale have large effects:

| Hit ratio | Requests reaching the database, per 10,000 |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| 90%       | 1,000                                      |
| 95%       | 500                                        |
| 99%       | 100                                        |
| 99.9%     | 10                                         |

A drop from 99% to 98% looks minor on a dashboard, yet it doubles database load. This is why a small change, such as a new field in the cache key or a shorter [TTL](node:TTL), can produce a database incident with no increase in traffic.

Hit ratio also drives average [latency](node:Latency). If a hit takes 1 ms and a miss costs 1 ms for the check plus 50 ms for the database, a 90% hit ratio averages 6 ms and a 99% ratio averages 1.5 ms.

Several things commonly lower the ratio: keys that include a timestamp or request ID, so that nothing repeats; a cache too small for its working set, the data in regular use; and restarts or deploys that leave the cache empty. Adding nodes with naive hashing has the same effect, which [consistent hashing](node:Consistent%20hashing) avoids.

Read the number with care. A single overall ratio can hide one important endpoint at 40% behind many trivial lookups at 99.9%, so measure it per key type. A high ratio also says nothing about whether the data served is correct.
quotes: Database CPU doubled after the release, but traffic is flat.
Cache hit ratio fell from 99 to 98. The new locale field in the key split every entry.

nodes.name: Cache-aside
nodes.description: A caching pattern where the application checks the cache, loads from the database on a miss, and stores the result.
nodes.markdown:
[Cache](node:Cache)-aside is a caching pattern in which the application manages the cache itself, loading data into it only when that data is requested. It is also called lazy loading. The cache sits beside the database and has no connection to it.

| Step | Path  | What the application does                     |
| ---- | ----- | --------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Read  | Looks up the key in the cache                 |
| 2    | Read  | On a hit, returns the value                   |
| 3    | Read  | On a miss, queries the database               |
| 4    | Read  | Stores the result in the cache and returns it |
| 5    | Write | Updates the database                          |
| 6    | Write | Deletes the key from the cache                |

The pattern has useful properties. Only requested data takes up cache memory, and if the cache goes down, reads can still reach the database, at the price of more load on it.

Writes delete the key instead of updating it because concurrent updates can land in the wrong order and leave an old value in place. Deleting forces the next reader to load the current value.

A race remains. Reader A misses and fetches the old row. Writer B updates the database and deletes the key. Reader A then stores the old value it fetched earlier. The cache now holds stale data with nothing scheduled to remove it, which is how a record can stay wrong for hours and then correct itself. Always set a [TTL](node:TTL) as a backstop, so that any such error has a limited lifetime.

Each miss costs three trips: cache, database, cache. After a deploy or restart everything misses at once, and a popular key that expires can cause a [cache stampede](node:Cache%20stampede). For data that must be current right after a write, compare a [write-through cache](node:Write-through%20cache).
quotes: One customer's plan shows the old tier, but the database row is right.
That's the cache-aside race. The TTL is a week, so shorten it and delete that key by hand.

nodes.name: Write-through cache
nodes.description: A cache where each write goes to both the cache and the database before the write is confirmed to the caller.
nodes.markdown:
A write-through [cache](node:Cache) is one where each write goes to both the cache and the backing database before the caller receives confirmation. Because the two are updated as part of one operation, a read that follows a successful write finds the new value in the cache.

| Step | Who      | What happens                               |
| ---- | -------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| 1    | App      | Sends the write to the cache layer         |
| 2    | Cache    | Stores the new value                       |
| 3    | Cache    | Writes the value to the database and waits |
| 4    | Database | Confirms the write                         |
| 5    | Cache    | Confirms success to the app                |

Some products provide this behaviour directly. With a plain store such as Redis, the application usually performs both writes itself, which gives weaker guarantees, because a crash between the two leaves them different.

This pattern addresses a common complaint with [cache-aside](node:Cache-aside): a user saves a change and the next read is a miss or returns something old. Recently written data is already cached, so reads of recent data are fast and current.

The costs fall on the write path. Each write now waits for two systems, so write [latency](node:Latency) is at least that of the database, and it does nothing to reduce database write load. A [write-heavy workload](node:Write-heavy%20workload) gets little benefit. The cache also fills with data that may never be read, such as records created once and left alone, so pair it with a [TTL](node:TTL) or an [eviction policy](node:Eviction%20policy).

Failure handling needs a decision. If the database write fails, the cached value must be removed or never exposed, or readers will see data that was never saved. Other systems that write directly to the database also bypass the cache and leave it stale, so route all writes through the same path.
quotes: Users edit their profile and sometimes see the old name for a few seconds.
Profile reads vastly outnumber edits, so a write-through cache fits. The extra few milliseconds on save won't matter.

nodes.name: Write-behind cache
nodes.description: A cache that confirms a write immediately and saves it to the database later, trading durability for write speed.
nodes.markdown:
A write-behind [cache](node:Cache) confirms a write as soon as it holds the value, then saves it to the database later in the background. It is also called a write-back cache. The caller gets a fast response, and the database receives the change some time afterwards.

The three common write strategies differ in when the database is updated:

| Pattern                                     | Database updated     | Write speed               | Risk of data loss |
| ------------------------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------- |
| [Cache-aside](node:Cache-aside)             | By the app, on write | Database speed            | Low               |
